subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO REVIEW RAILWAY PROBLEMS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO REVIEW RAILWAY PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into problems relating to railway transportation and the alleviating of inequities in the freight rate structure. A little later I shall ask leave to table two copies of the order in council which establishes this commission.
Hon. members will recall that the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green), as Acting Prime Minister, on November 26 announced the intention of the government to set up a suitable body to review the general field of railway problems and policy. He said this study would include not only a comprehensive consideration of the freight rate problem, including the situation of the long haul provinces in the west and in the Atlantic region, but also other specific problems which required solution if Canada's railways were to be able to serve the national interest without prejudicing particular areas or industries.
At the same time it was announced that pending the results of this long term study, measures would be worked out to relieve inequities in the freight rate structure, and this, of course, has been done in Bill C-38, now before the house, which is designed to carry out that intention. I think an examination of the terms of the commission will make clear that they are wide enough to cover all that is necessary and specific enough to direct the attention of the commission to the most urgent problems.
I should like to refer to the powers in general, which are as follows:	The commission is empowered to inquire into and report upon the problems relating to railway transportation in Canada and the causes thereof and to recommend solutions thereto; and in particular, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, the commission shall consider and report upon:
(a)	inequities in the freight rate structure, their incidence upon the various regions of Canada, and the legislative and other changes
that can and should be made in furtherance of national economic policy to remove or alleviate such inequities;
(b)	the obligations and limitations imposed upon the railways by law for reasons of public policy, and what can and should be done to ensure a more equitable distribution of any burden which may be found to result therefrom;
(c)	the possibilities of achieving more economical and efficient railway transportation;
(d)	whether and to what extent the Railway Act should specify what assets and earnings of railway companies in businesses and investments other than railways should be taken into account in establishing freight rates; and
(e)	such other related matters as the commissioners consider pertinent or relevant to the specific or general scope of the inquiry.
The commission will consist of the following: Hon. Charles P. McTague, Q.C., Ll.D., chairman; Herbert Anscombe of Victoria; Archibald H. Balch, Ottawa; Rene Gobeil, Quebec city; M. A. MacPherson, Sr., Q.C., of Regina; Howard Mann of Moncton and Arnold Platt of Lethbridge. We think those recommended have the necessary qualifications. Mr. McTague, Mr. MacPherson and Mr. Anscombe are, of course, widely known. Mr. Balch is chairman of the national legislative committee of the national railway brotherhoods. Mr. Gobeil is a consulting engineer. Mr. Howard Mann of Moncton is secretary of the maritime transportation commission, and Mr. Arnold Platt is a farmer and immediate past president of the Alberta farmers union.
The commissioners are aware that it is the desire of the government, and I am sure of parliament, that they should proceed with this inquiry with all reasonable dispatch in order that a report may be made on these important problems as soon as it is possible to assemble and consider all the information and analyses that it is necessary to have.
When the Minister of Public Works as acting prime minister announced the government's intention to arrange for this review he assured the western farmers that such review would not mean that they would have to pay more freight on the shipment of grain for export. I wish to take this occasion to confirm this, in regard particularly to the action that may be taken as a result of the work of the royal commission. To make it

Royal Commission on Railways clear beyond question, the Crowsnest pass rates are part of a bargain that was made between the railways and the government on the one hand and the settlers who went west on the other hand. We intend, in so far as this government is concerned, to see to it that that contract shall not be broken. I wish to table, sir, copies of P.C. 1959-577.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO REVIEW RAILWAY PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house welcome the announcement by the Prime Minister of the appointment of a royal commission to inquire into transportation matters. While it is difficult at this time to analyse what the powers of the commission are, this will be possible after we have been able to consult Hansard.
However, as I listened to the Prime Minister I was impressed with the powers which the government intends to give to this commission, namely powers which will authorize the commission to investigate not only the inequities in the freight rate structure but also the transportation problem in general.
The house will remember that the Prime Minister invited some of us on this side to make suggestions to him as to the subjects to which consideration should be given by the commission. Whether or not these recommendations have been taken into consideration it is not possible for me to say from the statement the Prime Minister has made. 1 think there is no doubt, sir, that an investigation into the whole transportation problem of this country, that is the railway transportation problem, and into the freight rate structure is imperative at this time.
I would, however, like to remind the government that similar investigations were made by the former administration in years past. I should like to bring to the attention of the government the fact that under P.C. 1487 there was conducted a complete and thorough investigation of the freight rate structure. The board of transport commissioners has handed down three reports in that connection. Then there was the Turgeon royal commission which followed and which made a number of important recommendations all of which, in so far as the freight rate structure of this country is concerned, were implemented by the former administration by way of legislation.
There may be, however, a series of circumstances that have developed since that time which make it important and imperative that further investigation be carried out. The government has seen fit to do that, and we on this side of the house welcome it. May I, however, say to the Prime Minister,


in view of the statement made by the Minister of Transport and I believe by the Acting Prime Minister in the absence of the Prime Minister, that time is of the essence in connection with any investigation of this nature. I say that having regard to the fact that there is now pending, although it is adjourned, before the board of transport commissioners an application for a further increase of some 12 per cent in freight rates.
Whether or not it will be possible for this commission to report within the period of a year I am not in a position to say. But I do know this, that having regard to what the Turgeon commission did-and they made a very thorough investigation of the transportation problem-it took them two and one half years. It would seem to me that if this commission is to do the kind of job that parliament expects it to do, it should take all the time that is necessary.
I thought I should put these suggestions or this reaction to the announcement on Hansard because there can be no doubt that all of us agree that this is all to the good. In connection with the last statement made by the Prime Minister concerning the Crowsnest rates, I may add that I believe he will remember that on more than one occasion when I occupied the post of minister of transport I stated that there was no intention on the part of the then government to alter in any way the status of these rates which had been established in 1897.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO REVIEW RAILWAY PROBLEMS
speechtext:
The
present injustices and inequities and the many problems that face the various regions in Canada, particularly certain sections of industry and agriculture, have required investigation for some time. On that account we in this group are glad to know that the government has appointed this royal commission to investigate this section of the transportation problem.
We are sorry, Mr. Speaker, that the royal commission has not the power to investigate all aspects of transportation including air, sea and road, because we believe that the evolution of a satisfactory transportation policy means an investigation into all aspects of transportation and the tying of them together by one investigation, one report and one set of recommendations.
To that extent, Mr. Speaker, in our opinion the royal commission has been shackled. However, we trust that the commission will speedily undertake its duties and that a report will come forward at the earliest possible time in order that legislation may be presented to this house at the soonest possible moment.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house that discussions took place in Ottawa last week between the aeronautical authorities of the United Kingdom and Canada, with a view to bringing up to date the air agreement signed in August, 1949 between the two countries. The problems confronting the two governments on the next phase of international transport were examined, and it was decided that the traffic rights under the present bilateral should be broadened to meet the new situation.
The United Kingdom granted Canada the right to originate flights in Toronto destined for Hong Kong; to originate flights in western Canada destined for the United Kingdom; and rights in Europe between London, Brussels, Dusseldorf, Zurich and Vienna. Canada granted the United Kingdom rights in Toronto on the north Atlantic service. The air lines of both countries will be able to exercise the new rights on March 1, 1960.
I am very pleased with the outcome of the discussions with the United Kingdom, and expect that the new services will greatly contribute to the convenience of the travelling public.

subtopic: BILATERAL AGREEMENTS ON PEACEFUL USES
BILATERAL AGREEMENTS ON PEACEFUL USES
speechtext:
1.	Are negotiations underway at present between Canada and any other government or governments, with a view to a bilateral agreement on the peaceful uses of atomic energy?
2.	If so, with which countries?
3.	What form are any such negotiations taking?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: BILATERAL AGREEMENTS ON PEACEFUL USES
speechtext:
The answer to the first question is yes.
The answer to the second question is: Japan, Pakistan, Australia and the European atomic

energy community, known as EURATOM. The members of EURATOM are Belgium, Federal Republic of Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.
The answer to the third question is: In the case of Japan, a Japanese delegation has been meeting in Ottawa with Canadian government officials. The negotiations with EURATOM were conducted initially by a Canadian delegation sent to Brussels for this purpose and are being concluded by the Canadian embassy in that city with the EURATOM commission. The other negotiations have been taking place through normal diplomatic channels.

DEGREE GRANTING
speechtext:
1.	Is Royal Military College a degree-granting institution?
2.	If so, does its charter authorize the granting of honorary degrees?
3.	Who recommends candidates for honorary degrees?
4.	Have any candidates been recommended for such degrees?
5.	If so, who are they?
6.	What qualifications must any candidate for an honorary degree possess?
7.	Is Royal Military College under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence?

speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: DEGREE GRANTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first two questions, the Royal Military College of Canada is a degree granting institution by virtue of The Royal Military College of Canada Degree Act. Section 2 of that act reads:
The senate of the college shall have the power to grant degrees and honorary degrees.
In answer to question 3, I suppose normally the recommendations would originate with the senate, but I know of no restrictions to prevent anybody making a recommendation to the senate.
In reply to questions 4 and 5, I am sure hon. members of the house will be very pleased to

learn that, on the recommendation of the senate, on Friday of this week Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker will have an honorary degree conferred upon him. He is, as all hon. member know, Prime Minister of Canada, a member of Her Majesty's privy council, a distinguished member of the Canadian bar, and a gentleman who served overseas with the Canadian expeditionary force during the years 1916 and 1917.
In reply to the sixth question, I think the general answer is that the Royal Military College follows the normal practice of other universities in considering candidates for honorary degrees.
In reply to the seventh question, the answer is yes.

speechtext: The hon. member for Essex East.

subtopic: AUTOMOBILES
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCE ON MANUFACTURE OF SMALL CARS
speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Following the presentation made to the cabinet by the united automobile workers last month on the matter of small cars, is the Prime Minister in a position at this time to make a statement on the subject?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AUTOMOBILES
subsubtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CONFERENCE ON MANUFACTURE OF SMALL CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for some months there have been newspaper reports to the effect that the so-called big three in the United States motor car industry were planning to produce small cars in the United States. Following these reports a delegation of the united automobile workers had a conference with the government urging that, if such reports were correct, small cars should also be produced in Canada. Prior to the visit of the delegation the government had been giving consideration to this matter and discussions have been going on between the government and its officials with representatives of the automobile industry.
I can say this, that if and when Ford, General Motors or Chrysler announce that they intend to enter upon the production of the so-called small cars in the United States the government is determined, in so far as lies within its power, to have smaller cars produced in Canada.
To that end I have asked the presidents of General Motors of Canada, Ford and Chrysler to meet with me in Ottawa on Saturday morning when discussions will take place. Following these discussions I hope I will be in a position to determine, with my colleagues, the future course to be taken. But let me emphasize that if small cars are manufactured in the United States by these companies we want the same situation in Canada.

The house resumed from Tuesday, May 12, consideration of the motion of Mr. Starr for
Unemployment Insurance Act the second reading of Bill No. C-43, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rather thought from the challenges that had been made in the debate so far that perhaps the first speaker this afternoon would have been the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) explaining to us the reasons for the extraordinary financing that the cabinet has seen fit to provide for the unemployment insurance fund, which everybody knows is a fund which has about $400 million worth of securities in its portfolio. I am not going to comment further about that. I hope that before the debate concludes the minister will explain, not only the authority but the reason for this unusual and unprecedented form of governmental intervention in the affairs of a fund that is basically contributed to by non-government sources. Eighty per cent comes from employees and employers.
My chief point at this time, Mr. Speaker, is to direct the attention of the house to the fact that in the last couple of years, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) himself said, we have had an unusual experience in that the amount of money paid out has greatly exceeded the amount of receipts. Of course, that is typical of any insurance scheme, at unusual times but the question which I want to raise before the house at this time is the question of whether or not the act, as it now stands, is really satisfactory to members of this house having regard to investment policy. I will be the first to say that this particular legislation was provided by the previous administration; but under the previous administration we had not the same experience of take-outs from the fund as we have had recently. I confess, that section 85 of the statute stipulates that the funds of the unemployment insurance commission should be invested exclusively in government of Canada securities.
Then under section 20 there is set up what is called an investment committee. Having regard to the experience of the last couple of years and the startling information that there have been capital losses of over $10 million-perhaps more, but the latest return was $10 million-I wonder if the house in considering this act would not want to make sure that a review should take place with respect to the set-up of the investment committee as determined by section 20 of the act. I do not think that anybody who examined parliamentary return 8 2A, I think it is, of last session in 1958 would have failed to note that a high proportion of the investments of the fund were in victory bonds on March 31, 1958. But the interesting factor is that the people who are in charge of
3620	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act this very large capital fund happen to be the same people who have other responsibilities in connection with government debt policy and general fiscal policy. In recent times I am suggesting to the house that there could be on their part difficulty in deciding where their judgment should lie. According to parliamentary return 82A, which I mentioned, $402 million was invested in victory bonds. I cannot think that any committee member at that time could fail to foresee that there was a likelihood of greater need for liquidity in the assets of the fund; but on the other hand the same people who under this section are asked to be the investment committee are the very people who were associated with the Minister of Finance and others in the promotion of the sale of longer term government financing through the conversion loan.
In other words I see that these people are at times in the regrettable position of being asked to wear two hats. I believe that it would be highly advisable for the Minister of Labour and the government to reconsider this matter of the investment committee. In my opinion the investment committee in charge of a fund of these enormous proportions should be completely detached from the possibility of any conflict of interests with respect to the relationship of the policy of the Minister of Finance or the government in the matter of fund raising.
We have a precedent in the Canada Council. We have an investment committee there headed now by a private citizen, the much-esteemed former governor of the Bank of Canada. This bill is asking us to make sure that further amounts go into the unemployment insurance investment portfolio. While we are doing that I suggest we should make sure that the most impartial determination of best advantage to the contributors will result without question.
This is an unusual fund to the extent that it is not substantially government money. Eighty per cent of it is contributed by employees and employers. Under the act one member of the investment committee is nominated by the Minister of Labour but two are designated as being either the nominee of the Minister of Finance, or the governor of the Bank of Canada, or the nominee of the governor. Those who are paying 80 per cent of the shot, having regard to the disclosure of these capital losses, would I think feel better assured if we had an independent investment committee. I raise that matter for the consideration of the house.
We have been rather restricted in debate in discussing some sections of this bill. I am hoping that the committee on industrial


relations will not feel itself so restrained. I am hopeful that the committee will call for evidence about the possibility of widening the group of those who are insured under this scheme. This is a major factor but at this time the government has not seen fit to increase the number of those who could in all likelihood suffering this particular catastrophe expect insurance coverage. I feel the time is ripe for the industrial relations committee to examine the act carefully.
I am thinking of the possible inclusion of hospital workers and many other employees. Hospital workers alone number approximately 100,000. In view of the proportion of hospital revenues that will come from either provincial or federal government sources through insurance schemes I believe that hospital employees should be brought into this scheme. There are hospital maids and non-professional workers of various kinds who have not been included and I feel that the committee should give this question very serious consideration.
My main point, however, is simply to say that the experience of the last year or two indicates that the individuals who are responsible for policy with respect to the investment of funds in the unemployment insurance fund are the same people who in another capacity are engaged in debt management and other fiscal government matters. In view of the fact that 80 per cent of the contributions to the fund come from outside government sources-they are in essence taxes-I think a more independent investment committee is highly justified.
I would therefore at this stage move, seconded by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Garland), the following amendment:
That all the words alter "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house declines to give second reading to this bill which makes no provision for ensuring the stability of the unemployment insurance fund through the establishment of an investment committee independent of the persons responsible for carrying out the government's policies with respect to the public debt".

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE RATES OF REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I submit to you that this amendment is out of order. You will observe that it proposes that the house should not give second reading to the bill on the ground that the bill-and this is the language of the amendment:
-makes no provision for ensuring the stability of the unemployment insurance fund through the establishment of an investment committee independent of the persons responsible for carrying out the government's policies with respect to the public debt.

In shortened form, Mr. Speaker, this amendment proposes that the house should not give second reading to the bill because we have not included in the scope of the bill a provision which is not there now. When the Speaker was in the chair last evening he was called upon to deal with another amendment introduced on behalf of the official opposition which he ruled out of order. That amendment, if I may recall it to you, sir, was in these words:
This house declines to proceed with this bill because its provisions were formulated and introduced without any consultation by the government with the advisory committee and before receiving the annual report of that advisory committee on the financial condition of the unemployment insurance fund for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1959, and its recommendations thereon.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that you were not in the chair at the time, that the ground upon which the Speaker ruled that amendment to be out of order was that on second reading an amendment that can be submitted and be in order is an amendment that sets up a contrary principle, a principle contrary to the principle of the bill. It was quite evident to the Speaker, in dealing with the amendment introduced last evening, that it did not introduce a principle contrary to the principle of the bill. It dealt with something that the opposition argued was antecedent to the introduction of the bill, something that should have been done before the bill was brought before the house, that there should have been prior consultation, that the bill should not have been submitted until a certain report had been received. In view of the nature of the amendment he ruled that it did not set up a principle contrary to the principle of the bill, and therefore he ruled it out of order.
Now, that rule, Mr. Speaker, is obviously one aspect of the rule of relevance. My submission to you with respect to this new amendment, is that it fails for the same reason and is not relevant to the bill before you. The bill before you contains a number of amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, in designated clauses of that act. None of these clauses relates to the subject matter of this amendment.
In his remarks in leading up to the introduction of his amendment, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) referred to the provisions of section 20 of the main act which determines the composition of the investment committee. Then he made reference also to the later sections of the act, sections 85 and 86. None of these sections, Mr. Speaker, falls within the scope of the amending bill now under debate, Bill No. C-43.
Unemployment Insurance Act
Last night the Speaker had occasion to refer not once but several times to the well-established rule that the introduction of a bill to amend a statute in this house does not in fact open up the entire statute for discussion in this house, and discussion on the amending bill must be relevant to the bill and cannot stray outside the scope of the bill into the wider provisions of the statute which it proposes to amend. This is precisely what has been done here this afternoon.
There is nothing in the present bill at all that concerns or affects the composition or the powers of the investments committee. There is nothing in the amending bill, which relates to investments, and yet the amendment before you proposes that the house should withhold second reading of this bill because it makes no provision for changing the provision of the main act in reference to the investment committee.
If this amendment were in order it would be possible for any member to discuss any provision of the main act, regardless of whether it receives mention or no mention in the amending bill. It would be equally competent to any member to introduce any amendment proposing that second reading of the bill be withheld because some provision of the main act, not mentioned in the amending bill, is not included within the scope of some particular amending provision. This would reduce the procedure of the house obviously to chaos, and it is because of considerations of this kind that the rule is so well established: first, that the introduction of an amending bill does not open up the main statute for discussion and debate; second, that any amendment must be strictly relevant to the bill. The fact that it concerns some provision of the main act does not make it at all relevant to the bill. In the third place, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that this amendment does not set up a principle contrary to the principle of the bill. It says only that the bill should not be read now because it does not make provision for something that lies outside of it. Obviously, Mr. Speaker, this amendment is out of order on several grounds and I respectfully ask you so to rule it.
Mr. W. M. Benidickson (Kenora-Rainy
River): On the point of order, may I just refer to the matter of relevancy? Your Honour will have looked at the remarks of the Speaker the other night when he referred to principles of an amending bill. I think that is of the essence here. We are being asked to vote additional moneys to this fund. This amendment relates entirely to those moneys and I say that that therefore is one of the basic principles of the bill. I

Unemployment Insurance Act refer to the principle of stability of the fund or the integrity of the fund, as I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) called it the other night. It is of the essence to make sure that the investment policy will maintain stability and integrity in the fund.

If you
would allow me, Mr. Speaker, I should like to supplement what the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has said in this connection. This matter has interested me and I thought I would engage myself this morning in looking up the appropriate authorities which I think clearly establish the false position in which the Minister of Finance seeks to place us when he calls Your Honour's attention to an amendment which had been ruled out of order last night. But, as he himself indicated in the remarks which he made this afternoon, there is no similarity between the amendment now before Your Honour and the amendment submitted last night.
I call Your Honour's attention to May's sixteenth edition at pages 530 and 531. At the bottom of page 530 I find the following:
It is also competent for a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move what is known as a "reasoned amendment". This amendment is to leave out all the words in the main question after the word "that" and to add other words: and the question proposed upon the amendment is, that the words proposed to be left out stand part of the question. A reasoned amendment is placed on the paper in the form of a motion and may fall into one of several categories.
(1)	It may be declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differeing from, the principles, policy or provisions of the bill.
(2)	It may express opinion as to any circumstances connected with the introduction or prosecution of the bill,-
And I underline the words "circumstances connected with the introduction".
That is a statement of principle which has been recognized by all commentators, including Beauchesne, who makes reference to a comment similar to May, in citation 382, which of course is well known to this house and which deserves mention at this time. Citation 382 reads:
It is also competent to a member who desires to place on record any special reasons for not agreeing to the second reading of a bill, to move as an amendment to the question, a resolution declaratory of some principle adverse to, or differing from,-
And I underline the words "or differing from". I continue:
-the principles, policy, or provisions of the bill.
And so forth. I shall not quote the remaining portion of this particular citation. Then if we look at the work, "A Parliamentary Dictionary", we find on page 162 what is meant by a reasoned amendment. In the

first paragraph on page 162 beginning with the second sentence I find the following:
This form of amendment-
Your Honour will remember that my hon. friend sought to base part of his argument upon his interpretation of what was a reasoned amendment.
-seeks, by substituting other words for those of the question "that the bill be now read a second (third) time", either to give reasons why the house declines to give a second or third reading to the bill, or to express an opinion with regard to its subject matter or to the policy which the bill is intended to fulfil.
My hon. friend who has just spoken has emphasized the argument of relevancy, and in that connection I would refer Your Honour to Votes and Proceedings for 1958 where there is a ruling by His Honour the Speaker on a problem involving this particular principle. The reference will be found on page 539 at the middle of the page where Mr. Speaker makes this observation with regard to the argument of relevancy:
This is the third time I have had to deal with this matter today.
I would call Your Honour's attention specifically to this observation. He says:
I will not repeat what was said previously. The first question which must be considered is relevancy. I think the Minister of Justice, in acknowledging that it would be relevant to debate whether the clauses of this bill are in conflict with our obligations under GATT, thereby acknowledges that an amendment directed to that same purpose is relevant, because if it is relevant to debate it-
That is the important point-"because if it is relevant to debate it."
-if the amendment is otherwise good-it is relevant to move an amendment declaratory of a principle to the same effect.
All through this debate, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has emphasized, emphasis has been placed in argument on the importance of preserving the integrity of the unemployment insurance fund. That has been the gist of most of the speeches. The particular committee referred to in section 20 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, modification of which is proposed in this amendment, has to do with that very argument, and if it is proper to make reference to such an argument and make it part of the main argument in debate, as Mr. Speaker has said, it is possible and justifiable to base an amendment on such an argument even though, as the Minister of Finance said, directly there was no specific reference in the bill. However, I would argue that by implication and indirection there certainly is.
The Minister of Labour himself has given us the justification for this amendment. He said that the purpose of the bill was to

maintain the integrity of the fund. The integrity of the fund can best be maintained by a proper investment policy. A proper investment policy is one pursued by the investment committee under section 20 of the act, and this amendment calls for a rearrangement and a new composition of that investment committee in order to do what the Minister of Labour said, namely maintain the integrity of the fund.
In this connection, if Your Honour will address himself again to May, page 421, 16th edition, he will find the author's comments on the question of relevancy, the matter I am now pursuing. There the author says:
The fundamental rule that debate must be relevant to a question necessarily involves the rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed. Stated generally, no matter ought to be raised in debate on a question which would be irrelevant, if moved as an amendment, and an amendment cannot be used for importing arguments which would be irrelevant to the main question.
Surely that is clear. The Minister of Labour indicated that the purpose of this bill was to maintain the integrity of the fund, and if we were justified in commenting on that particular purpose and now seek to strengthen the instruments by which the fund is to be made stronger, then surely this amendment must perforce be regarded as in order. Lest there be any doubt whatsoever, I refer Your Honour again to the words of Mr. Speaker at page 539 of last year's Votes and Proceedings where he goes on to point out:
The first question which must be considered is relevancy. I think the Minister of Justice, in acknowledging that it would be relevant to debate whether the clauses of this bill are in conflict with our obligations under GATT-
The amendment there had nothing to do, in the sense in which the Minister of Finance speaks with the argument in debate but since argument in debate was permitted by Mr. Speaker it must follow that the reasoning which he pursued in connection with that particular matter applies on all fours with regard to the matter now before us. The facts before us are that the unemployment insurance fund was diminished to the extent of $10 million as a result of the loss of value of certain securities held by the commission. That was a permitted situation as a result of the operations of the investment committee. We say that happened because the investment committee was improperly constituted and that because of these facts and in order to preserve the integrity of the fund the committee ought to have a different composition such as this amendment contemplates.
There is no precedent whatsoever against an amendment like this. All the positive 66968-9-230
Unemployment Insurance Act evidence clearly indicates that we satisfy the argument of relevancy. When my hon. friend says that there is nothing in the particular amendments before the house having to do with the investment committee he is right, but the point is, as the Minister of Labour said, that the purpose of the bill is to maintain the integrity of the fund and the only way that can properly be done is by an investment committee that is so constituted as to further that particular end.
For these and among other reasons I ask Your Honour to take the view on the basis of this argument that there can be no doubt whatsoever that this is a proper amendment, a proper amendment likewise for the reasons which caused Mr. Speaker the night before last to accept in principle the argument made in the amendment which I had the honour to propose. That amendment had nothing to do whatsoever with the sections of the bill. We were calling in that amendment for an increase in the contributions paid by the federal government for the purpose of giving benefits to the unemployed people of our country. There is nothing in the amendments which have to do with the federal contribution and to argue that this particular amendment is out of order is to argue that the Speaker was wrong on Monday when he acknowledged the amendment put forward at that time. So, Mr. Speaker, with confidence in this argument I submit it to you.

First of all, I must remind the house that we cannot compare the ruling which was made the other night by Mr. Speaker concerning the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) with the position of the present amendment. There is a marked distinction between this amendment and the other amendment, and the ruling which was made the other night does not serve as a precedent for the ruling which I now propose to make.
I have listened with great interest to the comments made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I have also listened carefully to the remarks made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), and the hon. member for Essex East. There are two points which I should like to emphasize. The first one is the question of relevancy. In the present instance, I consider that this amendment is not relevant to the bill being discussed. It is rather relevant to the act itself, but at the moment we are not discussing the act, we are discussing the bill. The second point I wish to emphasize is that the

Unemployment Insurance Act house should listen carefully to the way in which the amendment reads. I shall now read it:
This house declines to give second reading to this bill which makes no provision for ensuring the stability of the unemployment insurance fund through the establishment of an investment committee independent of the persons responsible for carying out the government's policies with respect to the public debt.
The way in which this amendment reads actually makes it more in the form of a separate resolution or bill than an amendment to what is contained in the bill under discussion. Then again, the rule of relevancy is completely disregarded. If every bill that was discussed by this house were subject to amendments of this type which could stipulate that the bill did not contain enough and should contain something else, then there would be no relevancy at all. I consider this amendment which is now before the house contains no reference to anything contained in the bill and I must therefore rule it out of order.

speechtext:
must admit that I find myself in some difficulty at this stage of second reading of Bill No. C-43 to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. I rather think I am in the position known as being over the proverbial barrel because I am damned if I do and I am damned of I do not, when it comes to a question of how to vote. Undoubtedly many cogent arguments have been set forth, not once but repeatedly, that there are sections of this bill which are of such a nature that they should be opposed.
There is a provision in the bill for approximately a 30 per cent increase in the charges on employers and employees so as to re-establish the fund or, as has been so aptly put by previous speakers, to maintain the integrity of the fund. I think it is obvious also that in so far as the beneficiaries of the fund are concerned, there is not a commensurate return from the 30 per cent increase in the charges which is to be levied in the future. There is also a section of the bill which introduces new and discriminatory taxation and to that, of course, I am certainly opposed.
In addition, I agree with the objections that have been raised that the increased charge is, in part, made necessary as a charge on the insured because of circumstances over which he had no control. I refer, of course, to the amount of money that was required to be taken out of what was actually an insurance fund to take care of the situation that arose because of serious unemployment, call it a recession or depression if you


like, and changes introduced by the government without any financial responsibility being accepted by the government which made the changes in the act. I think that is a negation of the principle of insurance and should not be supported.
There is also another matter, of course, which I think is very serious, and that is the fact there is no increase contemplated in the weekly allowances to those beneficiaries who fall in the low income categories. The amounts which they are receiving now are certainly low enough, and if the employees in the future have to pay increased charges and yet the majority of those workers will receive no increase whatever, then I think there is something wrong with the basic principles. As I say, Mr. Speaker, there are excellent and cogent reasons which have been put forward in great detail by a great many speakers in this house as to why there should be opposition to second reading.
At the same time there is another side of the picture. I find I am in agreement with the fact that some improvements are being made in the bill which is now before us. We have the bringing of new salary groups into the plan, and I think that is all to the good. There are small, very small provisions for an increase in the earning rates at the same time one is drawing unemployment insurance. Small as this improvement is, it is to the good. Then, of course, there is the extension of coverage. If one is eligible the period of eligibility is raised from 36 weeks to 52 weeks. Although I am rather inclined to believe that this will not cover a great many in the plan, it is an improvement without a doubt. For these latter reasons, therefore, I feel that the bill should be supported on second reading. You see, Mr. Speaker, what I meant on opening when I said I was over the proverbial barrel and damned if I did and damned if I did not.
However, an hon. member should, if he can act with conscience, vote, and so far as I am concerned a decision has to be reached. I have reached a decision, Mr. Speaker, based on this fact. If one turns down a bill on second reading which contains improvements which one favors, then turning down second reading in order to kill those things you do not like automatically deprives the people of this country of the opportunity of reaping the benefits of the improvements. The important fact is, and it is an important fact, if a bill does pass second reading, then every member of this house gets an opportunity to support those sections which he feels are improvements in the act, and at the same time he is able to speak against and vote against those measures of which he disapproves. There is such an occasion where

one can express an opinion on each proposal and each section, and that is when the bill gets into committee. Although I strongly disapprove some of the provisions and I think I also disapprove some of the motives behind the government's introduction of some of the provisions of this bill, nevertheless I also agree with some of the proposals and we will have an opportunity of expressing ourselves by speech and by vote in committee, and be able to try to vote down the things we do not like and try to get through the things we like. After being careful to explain that that is my position, as far as I am personally concerned it is my intention to vote in favour of the second reading of this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak briefly on this matter. The bill before us, which is one to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, seems to substantiate in my mind, two points. The first is that the government is prepared to accept the proposition of mass unemployment in Canada and the second is that it seems prepared to accept as a fact that unemployment will continue. In other words, it is apparent that this government, which claimed to have all the answers when they sat on this side of the house, are bankrupt of ideas for the solution of Canadian problems today. They are pursuing policies which, if continued, could bankrupt our national treasury. Mr. Speaker, it is apparent that the Minister of Labour and his colleagues have no policy to deal with unemployment. Instead, they seem to accept it by this legislation they seek to extract from Canadian workers and Canadian employers enough cash to pay for the government's folly. In other words, they are seeking to have workers and employers pick up the cheque for the failure of this government. The necessity for replenishing the unemployment insurance fund simply reflects the failure of this government to restore confidence in our economy, and failure to recognize and to attempt to cure the basic causes for the heavy drain on the unemployment insurance fund.
It is not my intention to deal at any length with these causes. They are well known, I think, to most Canadians: lack of planning; diversion of trade rather than expansion of trade; higher interest rates which are a drag on expansion and a drag on our economy; higher taxes, which retard and restrict expansion, expansion which can only come from increased savings and those savings from earnings. I think the people are wondering what has happened to this billion dollar program of public works. All of these things are, of course, the reasons, to a great degree, for 66968-9-230i
Unemployment Insurance Act the necessity for the legislation that is before the house at the present time.
But I rose today primarily to bring one matter to the attention of the government. I refer to the difficulty that is being experienced by many of our young people in Canada today in getting established in the labour force. I am talking particularly about those people under the age of twenty. They have been having considerable difficulty especially in this past couple of years. This is one of the most disturbing factors in our whole economy. It is one which is giving concern to many of the welfare organizations throughout our country and I think should now concern the government and business generally. I am not suggesting that this matter is solely the responsibility of the government but it is a very real problem.
I am going to use November figures which show a great difference between the impact of the recession on working people over 20 and its impact on those to whom I refer, namely those under 20. At November 15, 4.5 per cent of the labour force between the ages of 25 and 44 were out of a job and looking for work; but of the labour force between 14 and 19, 12.5 per cent were jobless. Mr. Speaker, I desire to say something about this bill on its second reading, which normally deals with the principle of the bill and which normally gives the opposition the opportunity to discuss, in a very general way, those principles and other matters relevant to the bill and all that it covers.
I agree, Mr. Speaker, with the government that something has to be done about the unemployment insurance fund, and I propose in the course of my remarks, with your permission, to deal with the situation which brought about this necessity and to deal also with the various methods by which this difficulty could be overcome, one of which has been put forward by the government in this bill. But that is not the only way of dealing with the problem, and indeed in our amendments, two of which were ruled out of order, we put forward alternative proposals dealing, as we thought, with the principles of the bills and its problems.
Mr. Speaker, as to the reasons which require legislation of this sort-I will come back to that again later in my speech-the statistical report on the operation of the Unemployment Insurance Act for March 1959, which has just come to my hand, gives us some very good evidence as to why the fund has to be strengthened, why it has to be replenished, and why the steps which the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) referred to in his brief address the other night have to be taken to strengthen the stability and the security of this fund which is so important to the workers of this country. This fiscal report includes, perhaps as its most significant fact, that unemployment for the 12 months ending March 31, 1959, according to benefits paid to claimants on the fund, was nearly 25 per cent greater than in the 12 months ending March 31, 1958. The total benefits paid out amounted to $479 million as against $385 million, the monthly average of beneficiaries being $452,000 for 1958-59 as opposed to $366,000 for 1957-58.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) that in approaching this bill and in approaching this problem we in the opposition, as the hon. member pointed out, are in a dilemma. There are some things in this bill which should and do meet with our approval. There are other

Unemployment Insurance Act things in the bill with which we strongly disagree; and there are some omissions from the bill which we think should be put in the bill.
There are also circumstances surrounding the introduction of this bill with which we most strongly disagree. Of course, that constitutes a dilemma. On second reading, as an hon. member said, you are confronted with a dilemma whichever way you vote. You are damned if you do and you are damned if you don't.
There are various ways of dealing with the problem which this bill attempts to deal with in one particular manner. There was an interesting editorial in the Financial Post of May 9 entitled, "Split Insurance Fund?" which puts forward one method of alleviating this problem. Perhaps I could place on the record one or two paragraphs from that editorial. Dealing with the draft bill before us the editorial said:
The proposal now is to raise contribution rates 30 per cent and to make a start at adding another huge group of seasonal workers to the fund-those in agriculture. This will simply mean that the industrial worker and employer will be making welfare payments to farm workers as well as to loggers and fishermen.
This is manifestly unfair.
I do not say that I agree with those words in the editorial. I continue:
An entirely new approach to unemployment insurance in Canada is needed. Perhaps we should not have one unemployment insurance scheme, but two. One could cover year-round workers and could pay its own way. The other could cover seasonally employed loggers, fishermen and farm workers and its resources could be beefed-up by drawing on the general funds of the state.
The government has not attempted to follow that course in the amendments to the act nor did the opposition in the amendments we put forward follow that course exactly. But we did put forward the view that the government contribution to this fund in the present circumstances-the proportion of the fund met by the general taxpayers through contributions-should be higher than it is at present. That was the principle that was embodied in the amendment we put forward yesterday. However, I agree, as I have said, that something has to be done. We do not think this bill is going at it in the right way although there are some parts of which we approve.
As I said, we strongly condemn the circumstances surrounding the introduction of this bill and this debate in the House of Commons. We believe that the procedures followed and those not followed by the government exhibit a contempt of parliamentary rights. That is all the more surprising in view of the language that used to be used by some hon. gentlemen opposite when anything

happened in this house that appeared to reflect on parliamentary rights and privileges. We think also-and this is one reason which would certainly justify any hon. member of this house voting against second reading of this bill-that there has been evasion or violation of certain of the provisions of the unemployment insurance act with which this bill deals. We think there has been on the part of the government a refusal which is to be condemned to provide the information on which to form an intelligent and reasoned judgment on the merits and principles of this bill on second reading. We are surprised, to put it mildly, that in this debate on second reading there has been no contribution made to this vitally important matter by hon. members on the government side of the house at a time when the level of unemployment is greater than it has ever been since the act was introduced.
The present debate has not been easy for the opposition. Hon. members opposite have certainly raised points of order which we believe has unduly restricted the debate. They have restricted debate by their interruptions and by the raising of these points of order. Yet no member of the government as yet has commented on any proposal made by those on this side of the house. We are always being charged by hon. members on the government benches with having no proposals to make. They say we are merely objecting. Yet we have not heard from any member of the government in regard to the proposals which were emphatically made by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) and which have been repeated by others.
The government has not yet answered the questions we have asked or given the information we had the right to get. Indeed, it would have been quite impossible for us to have conducted this debate with any sense of realism or of having covered the whole subject if we had not been able to secure after the debate began a report from the unemployment insurance advisory committee which has a definite bearing on the matters covered by this bill. I have said that I thought in this matter the government has evaded or violated certain provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Having made that statement which has already been made in this debate by my friend the hon. member for Essex East I should attempt to document it.

We also say that section 20 of the act has been violated by the minister. The orders in council to which I have referred provide for the loans to be repaid "from the proceeds of sale of government of Canada direct and guaranteed bonds at the sole discretion of the Minister of Finance or from the cash resources of the fund". Section 20 of the act states:
Investment transactions . . . shall be made only on the authorization of an investment committee-
It is our contention, therefore, that the governor in council may not determine terms and conditions which permit the Minister of Finance to say when and if securities held by the fund are to be sold. Under the act that is a function which belongs only to
Unemployment Insurance Act the investment committee, the personnel of which we think might be altered in view of existing conditions. I am not talking about personalities because the members of the investment committee as personalities are highly qualified men of great integrity but the composition of the committee, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), might be improved in the way he indicated in an amendment. So much for the violation and, as we see it, evasion of the act.
Let me deal for a few moments, if I may, with our contention that this particular bill with its amendments was introduced by the government without proper consultation, without the consultation which should have taken place with the advisory committee, and that we in this house have been denied information we had a right to have in order to appraise the principle involved in the bill. We all know, Mr. Speaker-I mentioned it a few moments ago and I repeat it-that the unemployment insurance advisory committee has the responsibility under the act to report on the financial condition of the fund. We all know that in July, 1958, they made a very important, indeed a unanimous recommendation dealing with ways and means of replenishing the fund, the very matter we are discussing in the bill. The committee repeated that unanimous recommendation of July in the hidden report of August, 1958. Yet, Mr. Speaker, in the drafting of the bill, in the discussions leading up to the bill, in the discussion of the resolution preceding the bill, in the discussion on second reading of the bill, in everything pertaining to the bill, and in the preparation of this legislation there was no effort made to consult or discuss with the unemployment insurance advisory committee at any stage so far as we know.
So far as we know-we have asked this question and it has not been answered- there has been no meeting of any member of the government concerned with the preparation of this important bill with the unemployment insurance advisory committee, which is also concerned with these matters, since the report made by the committee to the minister last August. In other words, the committee has been by-passed. The government did not even wait to receive the annual report of the committee on the financial condition of the fund before introducing this measure.
As a result of what we consider to be the arrogant attitude of the government toward the committee and of the silence of the minister concerned during this debate, we are asked, without sufficient information,

Unemployment Insurance Act to approve second reading of a bill to ensure the stability of this fund without knowing what is the exact financial condition of the fund. The only detailed information we have goes back to March 31, 1958, and this is May 1959.
Let me ask the government a few questions. What really happened to the fund during the fiscal year 1958-59? We do not know from the government. To what extent are the increased seasonal benefits responsible for the heavy drain on the fund? We do not know that. What were the amounts standing to the credit of the fund at March 31, 1959? We do not know that. What was the investment portfolio of the fund at March 31, 1959? We do not know that. When are we going to receive the answers to the questions asked by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin)? We do not know that. Yet, Mr. Speaker, we are being asked to approve the second reading of this bill whose main effect will be to increase the contributions of workers and employers to the unemployment insurance fund by, so far as we know, an average of approximately 30 per cent.
We have also raised another very important point in relation to the bill. It was done this afternoon by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I refer to the serious mismanagement of the fund during the last year which resulted in a loss of more than $10 million consequent upon the sale of government bonds at depressed prices. I suggest to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour that this loss could certainly have been avoided if the fund had carried a larger share of its assets in more liquid treasury bills rather than in long term government bonds. That loss was not avoided because of the fact that debt management policy, that is, considerations concerning the lengthening of the public debt and the conversion loan, had a priority over liquidity for those who had the responsibility of deciding the investment transactions of the fund. Yet, Mr. Speaker, the probability of heavy drains during last winter was evident before midsummer when the conversion operation was launched by the government. Such a mismanagement by the government of the contributions made by the workers and employers to the fund surely cannot be tolerated by the house even if it is designed to help the government temporarily to get out of serious financial difficulties.
I should like to say a few words now about certain specific provisions of the bill. As I said at the beginning, some of these provisions are desirable and we on this side of the house are happy to support them. We support them generally; we would support


them in isolation. We accept the idea of adding two new classes of benefits and of extending the maximum duration of the benefit period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks. We also approve the proposal to increase the amount of allowable earnings and to provide a higher schedule of allowable earnings for the insured unemployed with dependants. We are also ready to support the more generous treatment given in the bill to convicts which we would hope would help in their rehabilitation.
All these improvements may be-indeed, I think are-important in the case of certain individuals but on the whole and in relation to some of the weaknesses and dangers inherent in some parts of the bill we think that these improvements are marginal. These improvements are not going to impose a heavy additional burden on the fund because the benefits they provide are not likely to exceed $20 million annually. The Minister of Labour will correct me if I am wrong in these facts, because we have to make these calculations from the information which we have. We certainly would have liked to know from the minister his estimate for the new benefits provided by this bill, how much they would come to in dollars and cents, but up to the moment we have not been given any indication in this respect.
Also, Mr. Speaker, we on this side accept the creation of two new classes of benefits. Since we do that, we must also, to preserve the insurance principle which is basic to this legislation, favour the addition of two new classes of contributors at the top. The raising of the income ceiling from $4,800 to $5,460 can in itself, I think, be approved by us. It will bring in, and again the minister can correct me if I am wrong in my figures, about 80,000 more workers. These two changes, we estimate, will result in increasing revenues to the fund, but again the minister did not give us any estimate of the increased revenues to the fund as a result of these two new provisions. I would be very surprised, Mr. Speaker, if the additional revenue would be materially lower than the marginal benefits provided under the bill.
We, on this side then, would be prepared to support these particular, and some of them are minor, modifications to the act. On the whole, the increased benefits they provide would be offset by substantially similar increases in contributions resulting from the additional two new classes and the raising of the income ceiling.
But there remains, Mr. Speaker, what we consider to be the main provision of this bill, which is the general increase of all

contributions, as we have estimated, by 30 per cent on the average. Here again, the minister has not given us any detailed information on this, but we estimate it at a 30 per cent increase on the average, without any corresponding increase in benefits to the insured. We cannot, Mr. Speaker, accept that main provision of the bill. It is surely analogous to a further increase in taxes. If these provisions were accepted by the house it would mean $70 million to $80 million extra in contributions, and this is the important point, and 80 per cent of that would come from the workers and employers. We must not forget-we should not forget it because it has been mentioned in this debate more than once-the nature of this fund. Only 20 per cent of this fund is contributed by the general taxpayers through the government, and 40 per cent comes from the workers and 40 per cent from the employers; that is the nature of the fund. Yet the Prime Minister, speaking on the program "The Nation's Business" on April 20, had this to say, and I quote from the text of the broadcast:
-we will be paying out this year $550 million more to Canadians in national health insurance, welfare and social security payments, than in 1956-7. the last year before we came into office- that is to say, twice as much as the tax increases.
I should like to analyse that particular calculation, Mr. Speaker, but I am sure you would rule me out of order. When I quoted it, that does not mean I accept it. Then, the Prime Minister went on to say this, and it does have a bearing on the unemployment insurance fund and the nature of it:
The $550 million does not include additional expenditures which will be made for unemployment insurance as a result of the extension of these benefits to more people and for longer periods.
Then, he added this:
Here alone, the additional cost will be $200 million more than in 1956-57.
In other words, the impression was given that the government out of its beneficent generosity was adding a $200 million payment to the workers of this country. If that is the right figure, then 80 per cent of that is being contributed by the workers and by the employers, and the government dares to take credit for 100 per cent of the $200 million increase in unemployment insurance contributions, on the basis of a fund to which they contributed only 20 per cent. The Prime Minister found it necessary to repeat that statement in a speech which he made in Montreal last week.
Mr. Speaker, I conclude where I began. We accept the necessity for the replenishment and strengthening of the fund. We know why that necessity has arisen. It has arisen because of the high level of unemployment.
Unemployment Insurance Act As of March 31, 525,000 men were out of work, that is on the lowest basis of calculation, and 700,000 had applications for unemployment insurance. The Prime Minister, in dealing with unemployment in his speech the other night in Montreal, said that Canada had made a quicker recovery from the recession than other countries. One of the important indices of recovery from a recession is surely the figures for unemployment. What do they prove? They prove that in Canada, as of March 31, 8.6 per cent of our labour force was unemployed, whereas in the United States it was 5.3 per cent and in the United Kingdom, 2.5 per cent. So far as unemployment is concerned, and we are dealing with unemployment in this bill, who dares to say we have made a quicker recovery from the recession than any other country?
As I said at the beginning, some of the provisions of this bill we can approve, and some of the principles in this bill we cannot approve. We most strongly disapprove of the circumstances surrounding the introduction of this bill, the contempt of parliament which has been shown by those circumstances, the withholding of vital information necessary-

Question No. 3S1-Mr. Badanai:
1.	Is the armoury building in Fort William which has been closed since the middle of March, still being heated?
2.	Is the building going to be demolished in the near future?
3.	If not, what is the government going to do with it?
Answer by: Hon. Henri Courlemanche (Secretary of State):
1.	No.
2.	Crown Assets Disposal Corporation has advertised for offers for the demolition and removal of the building from the site with a closing date of May 20 for the receipt of bids.
